analysis.one_liner: Repeals a tax break for hardrock mining on public lands and uses part of the money to clean up abandoned mines.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee; no vote was ever taken before Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Mining companies that dig gold, silver, copper, and other hardrock minerals from federal public lands pay no royalties for the minerals they take. On top of that, they claim a percentage depletion tax deduction that lets them shelter a share of their income. This bill would end that tax deduction for hardrock mines on public lands, and would send a quarter of the new revenue into a trust fund for reclaiming abandoned mine sites — sealing shafts, treating polluted drainage, and controlling erosion.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would stop subsidizing mining companies' tax bills; and communities near abandoned mines, which would get a dedicated funding stream for cleanup of polluted water, unstable mine openings, and erosion.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near abandoned mines

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the percentage depletion allowance for hardrock mines located on lands subject to the general mining laws or patented under them, ending a tax deduction these miners currently claim [S2][S3].

It creates an Abandoned Mine Reclamation Trust Fund and appropriates to it 25% of the added revenue from the repeal, for Interior Department cleanup of abandoned hardrock mine lands and waters [S2][S3].
The fund can pay for sealing and grading abandoned mine entries, revegetation to prevent erosion and sedimentation, and treatment of water pollution from abandoned mine drainage [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies operating on public or patented mining lands, which would lose a valuable tax deduction starting in tax years after 2007 [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The tax increase applies to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2007, so mining companies would face higher tax bills that could reduce exploration and investment on public lands [S3].
Only 25% of the new revenue goes to abandoned mine cleanup; the remaining 75% is not dedicated in the bill and would be available for general government purposes [S2][S3].

Cleanup money is limited to sites the Interior Secretary determines have no continuing reclamation responsibility under existing law and that are uneconomic to re-mine, so many damaged sites would remain ineligible [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a widely criticized double benefit: miners take minerals from federal land royalty-free and also deduct a percentage of income as depletion. The main cost falls on the mining industry through higher taxes, with some risk of reduced domestic mineral investment; the main benefit is added federal revenue plus a modest dedicated cleanup fund. The design is narrow — three-quarters of the revenue is unearmarked and cleanup eligibility is restrictive — but the core tradeoff is straightforward.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill and sent it to the Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Feingold, joined by Senators Cantwell and Feinstein, introduced the bill on November 1, 2007 [S1][S3][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill remained in committee when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies kept the depletion tax deduction the bill would have repealed; taxpayers and abandoned-mine communities gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hardrock mining companies, which kept the deduction

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on November 1, 2007 and never held a markup or vote; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters were Democrats and the bill never reached a vote, so the broader partisan split was never tested [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Hardrock mining (gold, silver, copper and other minerals on public lands)
industries.note: The bill would repeal the percentage depletion deduction for hardrock mines on public and patented mining lands, raising these companies' taxes while they already pay no federal royalty for minerals taken from public land. Its interest ran against the bill's benefit to taxpayers.
